But while we were unable to grapple in an imaginative way with the housing problem, countries like the United Kingdom, New Zealand, the Netherlands, Sweden, Norway and others which had progressive governments

The Address[DOT]-Mr. Nicholson
were forced by public opinion to take advantage of the depression, and to see that, instead of'keeping people on doles and relief, something useful should be produced. Let me point out, in passing, that some of these governments were not labour governments; in fact, some were Conservative.
Of course, the production of houses is one of the most economic undertakings in which any country can participate. For instance, in the year that our building index was down to 9.7, in the United1 Kingdom they had' an index of 114.5.
For many years the leader of the opposition was premier of Manitoba. I would remind him that all the time he was in office disgraceful housing conditions existed in the metropolitan area of Winnipeg. I do not think housing conditions are any worse in Winnipeg than in most other cities, but in that city they have had a public health department that was not afraid to face up to the fact.
I hold in my hand a report of the public health committee for 1942. This is what Mr. Alexander Officer, who was so well known for years throughout Canada and who was chief inspector of the division of sanitation and housing in Winnipeg, had to say about conditions which prevailed in Winnipeg:
Surely our present housing shortage cannot continue much longer. The risk to health of our substandard housing, not to mention that of the fire hazard in our non-descript tenements, may be brought home to us with painful remorse. Already, we have much evidence in the toll of moral and mental standards, also the cost of crime in our blighted districts. Children are denied the elementary innocent amusements of youth, and are indeed, often exposed to health and moral hazards.
And further down:
The doubling up of families is one of the chief characteristics of slum areas and this condition is spreading like a cancer into some of our most exclusive residential districts. It is only a matter of time, therefore, when these districts will degenerate into blighted areas. . . .
Sliims have for centuries been the curse of large communities, serving as breeding places for all manner of crime and the spread of disease.
And at page 7 of the report:
It is surely not too much to say that when our men on active service return to civil life they have a right to expect that decent living quarters for their future family life is available, or at least in process of construction.
These are the conditions which, prevailed in Winnipeg when the horn, member was premier of Manitoba. If he was interested in providing housing for people in low income brackets, then something should have been done: by the provincial government for the city of Winnipeg at that time.
When the Conservative party was in office at Ottawa a special committee on housing was established. But it was not until 1935, not until it was clear that they were on their way out, that the committee was set up. Witnesses were called to review the situation. They reviewed conditions in Toronto, Halifax and Vancouver; they considered the cost of maintaining slums in terms of crime, fire hazards and disease. These matters are all set out in the report, but nothing very much was done.
Something was done. I was living in northern Saskatchewan at the time and we had some assistance from the federal and provincial governments in carrying out a housing programme. I mentioned in the house at one time something of the housing achievements of the Progressive Conservatives during those hungry thirties, and in looking through my old files I found a return that had been brought down in connection with housing assistance to three veterans in my constituency. One of these is a veteran of two wars. One sent two sons to the present war, one of whom will never return. The third served during the last war.
These three men who fought for freedom from 1914 to 1918 had committed no crime. They were carpenters who just could not get a job in Regina at any price, so they journeyed to the Hudson Bay Junction district, where I - lived, under a scheme financed partly by the city, partly by the province and partly by the federal authorities. According to the particulars furnished by the dominion authorities the following expenses were shared by the federal and provincial governments, both of which were Conservative at the time.
I shall not give the names of these veterans, but I have them here. Under the housing programme the governments of the day provided a payment of $6.70 for six windows. The next item is $3.80 for stovepipes, tar paper and hinges. The next item is $35.75 for lumber. The ceiling that was permitted in those days was $50 per unit, and you can see what a careful manager this settler was because his total expenses came to $49.75.
Of course, it should be remembered that all logs were free for the cutting. They were on a plot of land of 160 acres and so thick that you could not possibly drive through them, with your oxen. You did not have, to pay for the logs, but expert carpenters were obliged to go north; they were not forced to go north, but they came to the conclusion that nothing could be worse than living on relief in Regina. They thought that if they had 160 acres of free land, all the fuel they needed, some berries and maybe some wild game in the winter

The Address-Mr. Nicholson
time, if they would not be in heaven they would be better off. than they would be on relief in Regina.
Here is the next case-and I want to say that I know these families very well-which concerns a-father, mother and eight children. They were limited to $10 a month for food and were permitted to cut down on their lumber and put more into food. So this family spent only $31.60 for lumber. On account of having so many children they had to get along with fewer windows, and they had only $4.50 for windows. The total expenditure for the house was $36.10.
In the next case $5.45 was spent for windows and it is not stated how many. Then there was $5.85 for building material, $31.75 for lumber and $5.20 for tar paper.
As I mentioned, those were the houses that were built for heroes. These were settlers who came north in the thirties to try to get off relief. They were given $50 at a time when the governments of the day in Great Britain, the United States and Sweden were saying, "We cannot ask our people to live in $50 houses when we have plenty of lumber, plenty of building material and plenty of carpenters; our relief programme should be more ambitious".
I give this same reason for failing to support the Progressive Conservative amendment which, if carried, would amount to a vote of want of confidence in the present government. Who knows but what we might have them to take their place. Therefore I cannot support an amendment which says that the government has failed to take adequate and timely action to meet the ever-mounting housing crisis. I do not think they did that. I am going to support the C.C.F. amendment, but if that does not carry I shall not be able to support the Conservative amendment in view of their record while in office.
Coming back to the immediate problem, I must admit that the present administration has recognized that there is a problem. As I said, Wartime Housing was set up several years ago. While I was critical of the building of potential slums when permanent houses could have been built for about the same cost under some sort of plan, as I said, that is all gone and all the talking I could do would not change the situation. But I repeat that I think it was unfortunate that the federal administration should spend such large sums in building what have been called temporary houses and giving a guarantee that tihey would be torn down. Surely they must have known from past experience that these
fMr. Nicholson.]
houses will never be torn down so long as there are less desirable houses being occupied in Hull, Halifax or Vancouver. I am afraid that at the rate of travelling this situation will last for a long time.
In 1943 a special subcommittee on housing and community planning was set up by the advisory committee on reconstruction. The terms of reference were:
To review existing legislation and administrative organization relating to housing and community planning, both urban and rural, throughout 'Canada, and to report regarding such changes in legislation or modification of organization and procedure as may be necessary . . .
And so on. If hon. members have not read this report I urge them to do so, because I think it one of the best pieces of work done by the groups working on reconstruction. It is certainly the best study by far that has been done to date on the housing problem in Canada The recommendations are set forth ih an easily read fashion at the commencement of the book. They review conditions in different parts of Canada; they deal with urban housing, rural housing and legislation in other countries. Nothing less than the carrying out of the recommendations of this subcommittee will be good enough in this day and age.
In 1944 the National Housing Act was brought down, supposedly to implement the recommendations in this report. This act has been in force for over a year and we must judge the government's performance by the results to date. I think it should have been recognized that housing activities would provide one of the most popular and most useful post-war activities. Sir William Beveridge in his recent book on full employment says:
Adequate and healthy housing presents the largest single objective for desirable outlay after the war and affords the largest scope for raising the standard of life, health and happiness. Housing involves the setting up of a long-term programme of building to approved designs with the maximum of economy. The scale of the programme must be determined not arbitrarily but with reference to the total labour available; some forms of building and construction can be used as the balancing factor in the national man-power budget. The prospective importance of housing makes it vital to secure, by new methods if necessary, the maximum efficiency of the building industry. It is even more important to secure that national planning of town and country is made a reality, before permanent housing begins.
The legislation that has been passed has assumed that private enterprise would be able to solve the problem. The National Housing Act which had been in force previously was altered in several important details, but the fact is that the present National Housing Act

The Address-Mr. Nicholson
is just not of any use to people in the lower income brackets. What chance has the average worker in a war plant, a non-commissioned officer or a member of the armed forces who has been away from this country for four or five years to make the down payment and monthly instalments that gre required?
Our National Housing .Act is proceeding without sufficient consideration bejng given to town planning. Here, there, and everywhere houses have been built on lots without proper consideration of modern building requirements, and without consideration of the need which is everywhere recognized for town planning. Proper surveys have not been made to determine whether houses built under the National Housing Act are meeting the needs of the people who most deserve houses. According to the statistics that have been compiled eighty-five per cent of the houses built under the National Housing Act are designed for five persons or fewer. Is it the policy of this government to sponsor a housing programme designed to keep our birth rate low? The scheme operates without any large-scale administration to take advantage of reduced building costs. The programme also operates without adequate supervision of standards, without recognition of the interests of union labour, and without trying to find out whether the mortgagees would be able to negotiate the mortgages independently. There is no argument about it that those who have been able to take advantage of the national housing loans have been able to get their houses built at a much lower cost than they could have done before we had a national housing act. But providing cheap money or making lower rates of money available to those in the upper income brackets will not solve the problem in this country. That part of the programme dealing with low rental housing has been a complete flop to date. I noticed in the press yesterday a dispatch from Toronto saying that formation of limited dividend companies to finance the construction of low-rental housing projects throughout Canada w-ould be proceeded -with immediately by the Canadian life insurance companies as soon as a charter for the holding company, to be known as the Housing Enterprises of Canada, is obtained from the Secretary of State. I protest, Mr. Speaker, against a democratically elected government handing over to private corporations the responsibility of sponsoring the building of low-cost housing for the people of Canada. There is no country in the world where a scheme of that sort has worked out under private enterprise. The only countries that
have dealt effectively with slum clearance and low-rental housing have recognized that it is a national responsibility, that the federal government is the only authority that can adequately finance the problem.

speechtext: The United States, for instance. I suggest that hon. members take a trip and see what has been done in New York, Washington, and Pittsburgh. I am not suggesting that they have solved their problem in the United States, but at least they have demonstrated what can be done. In New York city, for example, one will find the Vladeck houses in one of the oldest districts, including Cherry street, where George Washington at one time had his residence. It was one of the worst sections of the city, one of its worst slum areas. New houses have been built there for 1,771 families, or nearly 6,000 people. They are living in modern fire-proof apartments, with running water, electric light, gas stove, electric refrigerator and modern bathroom. The rents range upwards from about S15 a month. The rents are a little higher in New York city; the average gross rent including services is $24.80 a month for the Vladeck houses, which is regarded by the people who live in them as a very low rental. But it would not have been possible for people to live in this sort of housing had it not been that some public authority realized that it is more costly to maintain slums than to face the problem and clear them.

Anyone who has visited the public housing developments in the United States, Great Britain or on the continent will agree that no private agency has been able to devise any scheme for building suitable houses and making them available to people in the lower third of the income brackets. In the United States the federal authority has popularized what it is doing. The pamphlet I have in my
The Address-Mr. Nicholson

hand shows what has been done, what these areas looked like before and after the projects were built; and if you go through these districts now which formerly were slum areas and see the children playing in the parks or playing in the recreation room in the basement, you will realize that for them the world is quite a different place from what it was before.
But in Canada we are passing the buck to the insurance companies. The act provides that municipalities, provinces and philanthropic organizations may contribute to a rent reduction fund-everybody under the sun but the federal government. But slum clearance should not be regarded as a charitable proposition. We must recognize that we have to pay for these slums directly or indirectly. We maintain our penitentiaries at a very high cost, and we have to provide fire and police protection for these slum areas. It has been established in many countries that it is cheaper in the long run to tear down the slums and rebuild to provide decent homes for the people. .
There are those who say that the working people would not appreciate decent housing. Hon. members all know the old slander about working people using the bathtub for storing coal. But there is not a single case on record in any country where working people have used the bathtub for a coal storage. On the. contrary, people living in the Vladeck houses in New York city appreciate the chance to have running hot water so that the kiddies can have a bath regularly.
Farm housing received a good deal of attention by the Curtis committee. The statistics compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics revealed shocking conditions in farm housing in Canada. To those who are interested in selling furnaces, radios and bathtubs I suggest that they should get behind those who are fighting for an ambitious housing programme. In Canada the percentage of farm people who have refrigeration, radios, automobiles, bathrooms, vacuum cleaners, is only 3-9 per cent. In Prince Edward Island it is -07 per cent; in Nova Scotia, 3-4 per cent; and so on down the way; a very small percentage. Like the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), I was born in a log house. Neither of us should apologize for that. Neither of us had anything to say as to where we were born. But my father and mother moved out of the log house as soon as they could, and I never once heard any suggestion that we should go back.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first like to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It is most appropriate that both the mover and the seconder, the one from English Canada, the other from French Canada, have come from the ranks of the heroic Canadians who fought and died at Dieppe, on the beaches of Normandy, France, Belgium, Holland and Hong Kong to safeguard Canada from the nazi hordes and the Japanese fascist militarists and to maintain the rights of the people of Canada to determine the destiny of this country. But I am sorry that I cannot extend the same type of congratulations to the government because of the lack of concrete proposals in the speech from the throne to meet the present emergency situation.
On the same day that the people of Canada read the speech from the throne, President Truman sent a message to the United States Congress outlining a programme for the people of the United States, to meet what he called a great emergency. There is a marked contrast between the two messages, the speech
from the throne and the message of President Truman. The president made one statement which I will quote, because I believe it is a basic statement of the type which we should have found in the speech from the throne, a statement which in a few words says exactly what is expected from governments at the present time:
The cost of transition from war to peace is as much a part of the cost of war as the transition from peace to war, and we should so consider it.
That is, we must consider the present emergency a continuation of war. and the same government responsibility that it had in the period of war in order to supply our men with arms, ammunition and everything else, the government must accept to-day. We have proved in the course of the war that we can do as 'well as the United States in all respects, in the field of production, of organization, and I do not have to say also, of course, on the field of battle. We can probably say that we in Canada blazed the trail in the matter of financing the war and stabilization. On some occasions when I visited the United States people told me that they envied our system of stabilization. If we could be trail blazers in war time, why can we not do the same to-day? Unless we work to-day in that spirit and unless the government accepts responsibilities in that spirit, military victory may be followed by economic disaster.
Everyone knows that the problem of reconversion is no simple matter. There are difficulties connected with it. We all recognize these difficulties, but the government should not try to hide behind difficulties. Instead of hiding behind difficulties and explaining away everything, it is necessary to tackle the problem in the same spirit in which we tackled problems in war time. Positive steps have to be taken to-day, to-morrow and the day after. It is the responsibility of the government- and these are not my own words; they are from the white paper-to maintain full employment and purchasing power. Basically to maintain purchasing power means to maintain war-time wage levels, to raise substandard wages, to provide means of livelihood for workers and their families in the reconversion period.
As I said before, in official statements of the government it is asserted that it is the policy of the government to maintain high income and high employment; but it is not enough to say that. Steps have to be taken, and rapidly, in order to make these things possible. It is -a fact that tens of thousands of workers who have been demobilized from the army, the navy and the air force, and
The Address-Mr. Rose

many thousands who have been let out from war plants, are being, forced by circumstances to accept wages far below war-time levels.
Surely this is not the way to maintain purchasing power. Men and women who are released from the armed forces and from war plants are not asking for anything extravagant. They want jobs at decent wages. If such jobs are not available, it is the responsibility of this government to provide them with a means of subsistance commensurate with a Canadian standard of living. I like that phrase, "Canadian standard of living". The trade union movement is unanimous in its proposal that the worker with a family should receive the sum of $25 a week during the period of reconversion, and * this is a perfectly justifiable demand. If any hon. member considers this an extravagant demand I would urge him to read the statement of President Truman on the same subject. I quote:
During this emergency every eligible worker should be entitled to twenty-six weeks of unemployment benefits in any one year. The maximum weekly payment for those workers whose previous earnings were high enough, should not be less than $25 per week.
Hon. members will see that those people who came here the other day were not, as some newspaper editorials stated, a bunch of radicals but were workers laid off from war plants asking for something which President Truman, who is no radical, also asked for.
Where is the money to come from for this undertaking? I know there is always that question. Well, there is $300 million in the unemployment insurance fund. If the government does not see fit to make an upward revision in unemployment insurance benefits the difference can be financed out of general government funds. Many workers have told me that even if this proposal were accepted by the government they feared they would be deprived of this benefit if they refused to take jobs at low wage levels.
The only condition for a man or woman receiving $25 weekly compensation should be willingness to accept work at a minimum wage recognized by the federal government as essential to the health and well-being of people. I emphasize that-a minimum recognized by the federal government-because we have in some provinces minimum wage scales which are a disgrace to Canada.
I have in my hand a reference book for the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction entitled, "Health, Welfare and Labour." On page 86 we find the following:
Weekly minimum rates for experienced workers under minimum wage acts.

What.are these weekly rates for experienced workers? I will start with my own province of Quebec. These are the provincial minimum wages: province of Quebec, zone number 1, which we are told is Montreal and district, twenty-six cents an hour; zone number 2, which is Quebec and district, twenty-four cents an hour; zone number 3, Terrebonne and area around it, twenty-two cents an hour; and other parts of the province, twenty cents an hour. Lest some hon. members from Ontario say this is only in Quebec, I want to disillusion them by citing the following for Ontario. In the Toronto area, $12.50 for female workers.

speechtext: An hour?

speechtext:
No, a week; and $11 in towns with a population of 5,000 to 50,000, and so on. I insist that this government cannot under any circumstances accept these as just and decent wage levels. These provincial minimum wage acts will not help to provide purchasing power for our people. It is true that at the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction this government indicated willingness to discuss with the provinces the setting up of national minimum wage scales, but this is definitely insufficient. It was the responsibility of the government to come before the conference and suggest a minimum wage which they believe is a Canadian minimum wage. In this matter the federal government should have given the lead to the country. They should have told the provinces what they regarded as decent minimum wages for Canadians. How did President Truman react to the same-problem? In the United States, too, they have constitutional difficulties, but President Truman did not hesitate to tell congress what sort of minimum wages he expected in the country. He said:
The goal of a forty cent minimum was inadequate when established. It has now become obsolete. ... I therefore recommend that the congress amend the Pair Labour Standards Act by substantially increasing the minimum wage specified therein to a level which will eliminate substandards of living, and assure the maintenance of the health, efficiency and general well-being of workers.
That is a different sort of language from what we find in the speech from the throne. I do not believe it is too late now for the government to go before the next session of the dominion-provincial conference and state what they believe a national minimum should be. There are constitutional difficulties, it is true, but the fight for a national minimum must be started some time, and the time is now. By giving such a lead, the government at the same time will discourage certain employers from going in for some terrific wage

The Address-Mr. Rose
slashes; and if any hon. member doubts that such a practice is being followed at the present time in Canada, or that there are certain employers bad enough to think we should have wage cuts now, I want to quote a statement I found in the Montreal Standard of September 1, 1945, made by Victor M. Drury, president of Canadian Car and Foundry. He is quoted as saying:
The party is over. Not only will there not be enough jobs, but wages will have to be brought down to former peace-time levels. If the employees won't take a cut in wages, the plant will have to close down. We can't afford to have our profits cut into by paying the high war-time wage levels.
At the same time, according to the Standard, Mr. Drury admitted that the average take-home pay of his worker's at no time was more than $28 a week.
After reading that statement in the Standard I decided to look into the figures of profits of various companies, and of course I was interested in Canadian Car and Foundry. After taxes and depreciation the net profits of this company were as follows:
1941		 $ 700,000
1942		 950,000
1943	  830,000
1944	  1,130,000
So I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whose party was
it?
It is because there are employers of this type that labour needs greater protection on the part of this government. Of course primarily it will be up to the workers and their organizations to fight for what they want, but they also need protection on the part of the government. Therefore this government should help the labour movement achieve a forty-hour week (but with no cut in take-home pay so that there will be fewer unemployed), union security, and other measures that will help to maintain purchasing power.
In the speech from the throne this government speaks of a high level of employment. Here again I wish to say that we fall short of what President Truman gives as an objective for the people of the United States. He speaks about full employment, not high employment, and he has called upon congress to pass a full employment bill now before it. I have that measure before me to-night; it is known as the Murray-Wagner bill, and I want hon. members to listen attentively while I read from it, because we can afford to copy it, and not only to copy it on paper but to fight for it:
All Americans able to work and seeking work have the right to useful, remunerative, regular and full-time employment, and it is the policy of the United States to assure the existence at all times of sufficient employment opportunities
to enable all Americans who have finished their schooling and who do not have full-time housekeeping responsibilities freely to exercise this right. . . .
How is it to be done?
To the extent that continuing full employment cannot otherwise be achieved, it is the further responsibility of the federal government to provide such volume of federal investment and expenditure as may be needed to assure continuing full employment.
Here they set down the responsibility in black and white, in a way that unfortunately we do not see in the speech from the throne or in any of the other statements made by government leaders. One of the ways to maintain purchasing power for the Canadian people is through public investment. Any programme of public investment must have as its aim the greatest possible contribution to the prosperity and well-being of the people, and I can think of no better investment than in homes for the people. In my first speech after coming into this house on January 26, 1943, I raised the problem of housing, because I saw that the situation was becoming more and more acute. At that time I called for the freezing of leases, and some hon. members thought that was not necessary. Well, since then the government has been forced to accept certain measures to which it would not listen at the time, but they far from meet the situation.
I am further reminded of the seriousness of the problem every time I return to my constituency. A few months ago a number of families living on a back lane came and asked me to plead with the municipal health authorities to allow them to remain in homes that had been condemned for the past twenty-five years, and were again condemned a few months ago. They were living in the centre of the city, with no electric lights and with leaking roofs. The situation was awful. I wenr to see those people in their homes and wondered how they could live there; yet they pleaded with me to be allowed to stay because they had nowhere else to go. Just before the opening of school this fall a French-Canadian woman came to plead with me to find a boarding house for her children. They were living in a store; she was ill and her children were ill, and they had to get out. The parents were going to take a room, and they wanted the children in'the boarding'home. Incidents like this can be multiplied hundreds of times throughout the country.
In this morning's Montreal Gazette we find the report of a meeting of a veterans' rehabilitation housing committee in Montreal, in

The Address-Mr. Rose
COMMON?
which the situation in respect of veterans returning from the armed forces is described as follows:
It has been revealed that approximately 300 men of the three services are being discharged daily in the Montreal area and that nearly twenty per cent of these are in urgent need of housing accommodation. Since this has been going on all summer it is now estimated that between 4,000 and 5,000 families are now seeking accommodation.
Without in any way minimizing the value of legislation enacted, it is obvious from these facts that the situation is not being met so as to provide homes for veterans, and for all who need homes, and to provide employment for the people. This government must decide to take the responsibility for the rapid construction of homes. This has been tried for a number of years but those who were to build homes have failed. We are not getting along rapidly enough. If Wartime Housing can build them faster, then Wartime Housing should build them.
The advantages offered to the limited dividend corporations should be extended to municipalities. The government should consider other means of cheapening the prices of houses and should make further research into methods of standardization. Experience has been gained in Great Britain and elsewhere in these matters. Perhaps the government can undertake to pay part of the taxes to municipalities in respect of newly built homes. It is obvious that much more drastic measures have to be adopted if the situation is not to become worse.
In tackling the problem of reconversion, I wish again to emphasize to the house that social security is an essential feature in any programme to maintain purchasing power. Money distributed by the government to individuals either to maintain them during unemployment or in their old1 age, or to maintain public health, helps the nation as a whole, as well as the individual receiving it.
From this point of view the proposals of the federal government to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction regarding health measures, and other matters, constitute an advance and a substantial step forward, and should be supported by all. Despite the fact that the proposals for a national health programme are not ideal, I believe they deserve support. If there is opposition from certain circles I would urge the people of Canada, through their members in the house and through their organizations, to do something about it, so that we may put out of the way rMr. Rose.]
those who would obstruct the application of the health programme offered by the federal government.
In respect to the problem of old age pensions I must be much more critical. I say that $30 a month does not mean a decent standard of living to anyone; and seventy years of age- that is a long time to wait. I would say that we need at least an old age pension of $50, and that it should be given without a means test at the age of sixty-five.
I know there are difficulties in connection with implementing the proposals offered by the federal government and some of those difficulties have been created by some of the provincial governments. I hope none of the provincial governments will stand in the way of the application of these health and other measures, so that action may be taken without delay. If some governments in the provinces refuse to go along with the federal government, then the government at Ottawa should be prepared to act in unison with those provinces which are now willing to collaborate.
The measures I have described might be described as domestic measures. But they are most necessary if we are to increase or to maintain the purchasing power of the people. Might I point out, however, that there are other means of maintaining purchasing power, and that one of these is the development of greater export trade. It is a fact that thirty per cent of our workers depend upon exports.
There is a great need for our products in many countries of Europe and Asia. But the . people in those countries cannot pay to-day. They must have long-term credits. From press reports I have learned that the government is contemplating substantial credits to Great Britain and France. This is good. Such a policy is in accord with Canada's needs, as well as our responsibility to those people who have suffered. But it is not enough. To keep our export industries working at capacity it is essentia! that Canada should also maintain all the other outlets, and create new ones in a number of countries, including Belgium, Greece, Poland, Jugoslavia, the Soviet Union, China and the Latin-America countries. We shall have to "step on it" to see that we help these countries to-day in their reconstruction, so that to-morrow they may be permanent customers for our goods, thereby helping to create work for our people.
In the remarks I have made this evening I have concentrated chiefly upon problems of reconversion, because I believe they are the key problems of the day. The manner in which the house deals with these problems will be the test of our ability to meet the problems of peace as effectively as we met the problems

The Address-Mr. Robinson (Bruce)
of war. We won the war because we allowed nothing to stand in the way of our war effort. We can win the peace if we approach the problem with the same determination.
I do not often permit myself to indulge in pessimism. I believe no hon. member can charge that I have done that. I wish to say, however, that unless the government meets the needs of the people in the present emergency we may find that we are heading back for the hungry thirties.
I should like to deal with a number of other matters, but in order not to offer any distraction from 'this key problem of reconversion I would simply add, in pas. ing, that I fully endorse the idea of a Canadian flag and of Canadian citizenship, and have so expressed myself in the house on other occasions.
There is one further problem upon which I should like to touch before concluding my remarks. This one deals with destruction rather than reconstruction. Every hon. member must have been impressed with the report of the terrible devastation newsmen found in Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It staggers the imagination of human beings to realize what will happen to our civilization if this dreadful weapon should ever again be used in war between nations.
We in Canada have a special responsibility in this connection because of the great deposits of uranium which are to be found in our country. If science succeeds in harnessing this mighty power to the service of human well-being. I am sure that as a nation we will gladly share this tremendous natural asset with the other peoples of the world, but until that day the potentialities of the atomic bomb for destruction- should not be placed at the disposal of any nation to use against other nations. I propose that this house and government place the uranium deposits of Canada at the disposal and under the control of the security council of the united nations organization, and under the control of that body alone. Such action will be more than a gesture; it will be a concrete demonstration of Canada's will for peace. Such action, along with policies aimed at full employment at home and generous assistance to our allies in repairing the destruction of war, will be a significant contribution by Canada toward lasting peace and prosperity in the world.
Mr. ANDREW E. ROBINSON (Bruce): Mr. Speaker, may I first offer my congratulations to you upon your election to the high office you now occupy. I am sure you will fulfil your duties as they should be fulfilled. To the mover (Mr. Benidickson) and the seconder (Mr. Langlois) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, who like 47696-121
myself are new members, I offer my congratulations upon the wonderful speeches they made. To our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) I wish, not continued success as a politician but health and longevity. To the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) I wish publicly to acknowledge my allegiance. To the hon. members of the political parties in this house I wish the best guidance.
I represent the county of Bruce and I am proud to represent that constituency. There can-not be many hon. members in this house who are not familiar with the good qualities of Bruce. During this session we have heard the Peace River district spoken well of by the hon. member for that riding (Mr. Low). We have heard about High Park from the hon. member from that riding (Mr. McMaster). I should like to tell the house a few things about my riding. First and foremost, Bruce is known o-ver this country as one of the best, if not the best counties in the dominion. Bruce has put forth a tremendous effort toward winning this war and the war of 1914-18; in men, money and materials we have contributed a great share. In the past Bruce has contributed greatly toward populating the western provinces, those provinces which have done so much toward feeding the hungry people of the world. Speaking as a Bruce boy, I must say that I am not too proud of the political trend that has taken place in some of these western provinces. To those who are thinking along the same lines may I say that they should not worry because these people are good people and eventually will see the error of their ways.
Not the . least achievements of Bruce have been the able men that the county has sent to the different parliaments of Canada, myself excluded. We are proud to claim the Minister df Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) of the present government as a native of our county. There are Senators Donnelly and Marshall who are active in the senate at the present time. In our town of Kincardine we are glad to have with us yet the Hon. Hugh Clark who for many years served our riding and the government of Canada in time of war. The late Hon. James Malcolm, who in his time was Minister of Trade and Commerce, was also a Bruce boy. We have no great centres of learning in our county, but we have produced many men and women who have made outstanding records in the business and professional life of the country.
At the present time there is in Ottawa a deputation of Indians, the original inhabitants of this country. They are here to have injustices removed and grievances corrected.

The Address-Mr. Robinson (Bruce)
In that delegation our Indian people of Bruce are represented. One of them is a sergeant and another a corporal who were in the same unit with me overseas in the last war. We had a platoon of those Indian boys in our unit and I feel safe in saying that there was not a better platoon in the Canadian army. We must remember that the Indians were here before we were, and the least we can do is to give them their just dues and the comforting assurance that their future welfare is in good hands. May I at this point read to the house a letter which I received from a corporal of Indian ancestry who is now overseas. This is from B company, first battalion, Regina Rifle Regiment, Canadian army overseas, under date of June 1, 1945, and reads:
To your letter of March 15, 1945, which I just received a few days ago due to changes of address. It took time for the postal corps to find me.
I have done you the favour asked by you. 1 myself have no use to, whatever party may be in. As to my status of civil life I am an Indian. I have no citizenship. All I have is a vote which is no good to me whatever. I have no voice in government, therefore my attitude to the government is poor. In the past I was looked down upon. It is what the future may bring can only change that, to change it from that. Can you give me some advice on what I could do in line of farming. Not that I want a big one. I want one that can bring me some profit, to be independent, to get by in every way. I understand the ups and downs of a farmer. Right now I am at wit's end. I am afraid to step into civic street. The setback f alie's bigger than the battles of the beachhead m Normandy.
I would be very grateful for any advice 1 may get.
I thank you.
Why should that boy not be given the chance of settling down on a farm under the veterans' reestablishment scheme without losing his rights and status as an Indian?
While Bruce county is the finest in Canada economically, we are not in the best position that it should be possible for the people of this country to achieve. For a number of years now we have not made the progress that it was our right to expect, due partly to the fact that Bruce is principally a rural county and agriculture is not getting its fair share of national income, and due partly to the centralization of industry.
At the present time, Canada has an acute housing shortage, but let me say, Mr. Speaker, that we have no housing shortage on the farms of Bruce county, and I feel safe in saying that Bruce county is typical of most rural counties all over Canada. To save the situation we must have decentralization, and to have decentralization we must revise transportation rates and power rates. By so doing we shall keep '

alive those centres like Bruce which have done so much toward building the country we live in and love. If consideration is not given to these facts Bruce, along with similar counties, will decline in population and in productivity.
It is nice to see our industrial centres grow, but if they grow at the expense of our smaller urban places and at the expense of our agricultural counties, we know that such is not good for the future of Canada.
Permit me, Mr. Speaker, to mention one of the greatest problems in Canada to-day, namely unity within our dominion. I believe that every hon. member is interested in finding a remedy. In this war it fell to my lot to have charge of a platoon of sixty men engaged in loading and unloading ships on the east coast. In that platoon were men from every province. Those men got along good together, and I believe that was the case in most units. The mixing up of those men from all over Canada will, I believe, help in the future toward unity; knowing each other's viewpoint will also help. To leam one another's language will go a long way toward solving the problem.
International good will is just one step on, a step that will ensure peace for the world. With the world machinery we have to-day it should be possible to arrange an exchange of scholarships throughout the world that would help every nation better to understand that we are all human beings.
I shall not criticize the present government, but I wish to state two facts: (1) The present administration did not have Canada ready for war in 1939; (2) in 1945 the present administration has not Canada prepared for peace. We all believe that Canada is the best country in the world. Let us get together and prove that such is so.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on behalf of probably the finest constituency in the Dominion of Canada.

speechtext:
Oh!
Mr. BROWrN: I am glad to see that hon. members agree with me. While we have a diversity of population, we have at least honesty of purpose. We are all hardworking, thrifty and sincere, and I think all hon. members will agree that we are a dynamic people.
I refer, of course, to the constituency of Essex W'est, and in particular to the city of Windsor.
I should like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to the, gentleman whom I have succeeded. I refer to the Hon. Norman A. McLarty, a gentleman and a scholar "who devoted a great part of his life to bis country and to his constituency in particular.

The Address-Mr. Brown
I should also like to compliment the mover (Mr. Benidickson) and the seconder (Mr. Langlois) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It makes me feel proud to be a Liberal to be associated with these fine young men.
I can not let this opportunity pass without paying a tribute also to the one who has done do much for Canada, one who has given, shall I say, his human sense of life to his country. I refer to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King).
I should also like to pay tribute to the men and women of the armed services. We shall never be able to repay them for what they have expended for us. We can, therefore, only make an attempt at giving some satisfaction. ' To you, Mr. Speaker, I extend my congratulations. You have already shown in your conduct of the proceedings of this assembly that you are being fair and conscientious.
It is interesting for me as a child in this House of Commons to sit here and listen to this debate. It is interesting from many points of view, because in this assembly we get the thinking of all parts of Canada. I shall not say what I think of that thinking, but at least it is an expression of what is being thought throughout the country. While some of our debate may seem frivolous or not very sound to the people at large, yet it is an expression that should not and, I am sure, will not fee curtailed. However, sir, I hope you will not think it presumptuous of me to take exception to a remark that was made in this chamber this afternoon. As I heard the remark, it was that politics "stinks to high heaven." Well, I agree with the speaker that probably in Alberta it does. But we in Essex county elect Liberals. I take exception to that, because I think there is nothing finer for a young man or a young woman in this country than to get out and take an active part in the public affairs of the nation. I feel sure that if we would all do that honestly, conscientiously and intelligently, there would not be so many political parties in the house. Politics to me is the science of government, and as such should be studied thoroughly by everyone. If that were done, the people, especially the younger people, would be more interested; we would get a more representative vote, and we would probably have better government.
I want to commend the proposals in the speech from the throne, in particular that with respect to the memorial by way of beautification of the city of Ottawa. Taking the dominion as a whole, and likening it to a human body or individuality, one can probably say that Ottawa manifests the mind or
the soul of the nation, for a nation we are; and as such manifestation it should be beautiful, complete and perfect. From a practical aspect, beautification would attract not only the constituents whom we represent, but people from outside our country, people who would come here to enjoy the beauty and to create for us a more friendly world. If we bring about that beautification of Ottawa there would be a certain material return, for I think we shall agree that the tourist business is one of Canada's largest industries. The human anatomy cannot be complete without the manifestation of the face, the eyes, and the limbs, and so it is that the beautification of Ottawa is not complete until we have a contribution from all the outlying parts.
Speaking on behalf of Essex West, we live in a district which has in front of its door more lake fresh water traffic than any other fresh water system in the world, passing by it. We have lake St. Clair at the north and lake Erie to the south. Across the river to the north of us-this may sound strange-* is the city of Detroit, for Detroit is to a great extent to the north of Windsor. Detroit, which surrounds us on three sides, has a population of about two million people. Two hundred and fifty miles away is the city of Chicago with about four million people. About a hundred miles away is the city of Cleveland; also near us are the thickly populated states of Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Illinois, and others. I do not need to tell the house of the population of that area.
We have in the city of Windsor, as I have said, a dynamic people. We have set up a town planning commission for the purpose of beautification and putting the city in proper order. The people of that constituency have an active art association, an active handicraft guild, and other cultural and literary societies and movements which express the thought of our people. What I am getting at is this: the city of Ottawa should be beautified, and I know it will be; but probably more tourists visit the city of Windsor and the county of Essex in one week than find their way to the city of Ottawa in six months. Being practical, I think we should try to capture a part of that traffic, not only for the material purpose of making money, but to let our friends see what we have, find out what kind of people we are, and cement the bonds of friendship which unite our two peoples. So that, I would recommend to this government that it consider ways and means of beautifying not only the city of Windsor but other ports of,entry; because when we regard the human anatomy,
War .and, Demobilization

the first thing we look at is the face, the eyes; and those ports of entry correspond to the face. Therefore, let us make those ports of entry spots of beauty which may attract tourists and help our common cause.
On motion of Mr. Claxton the debate was adjourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, September 14, 1945.
